title: Can AI chatbots write a good multiple-choice diagnostic question?
author: Craig Barton
summary: In the second of a three-part series, Craig Barton sets Gemini, ChatGPT, Copilot and Claude the task of writing a multiple-choice diagnostic question on adding 1/3 + 2/5, with each wrong answer exposing one specific misconception. He first shows his own question, answered over 20,000 times, as the benchmark. Gemini gives no correct answer and then muddles its reasoning; ChatGPT and Claude produce usable questions with some bad distractor explanations; Copilot mirrors ChatGPT, including the same hallucination and apology. Barton argues the task is harder than predicting misconceptions because the model must engineer a plausible wrong answer for exactly one error, and these systems are trained mostly on correct responses. His conclusion is a cautious yes: use ChatGPT or Claude for a first draft, check everything, and note that none can yet draw the diagrams most geometry and graph questions need.
points: A good diagnostic question needs each wrong answer to capture one and only one misconception, which is the standard the chatbots repeatedly failed.
The multiple-choice format lets a teacher gather every response at once with ABCD cards and read the nature of a misunderstanding from the particular wrong answer chosen.
Barton offers a reason for the weakness: models trained mostly on correct responses are poor at imagining how a student goes wrong, much like a novice teacher who only ever sat in top sets.
ChatGPT and Claude give a reasonable starting point and save time, but every output must be checked because errors are delivered with total confidence.
Since the chatbots cannot produce images, they cannot yet write diagnostic questions for graphs, bar models, loci or most geometry.
quotes: A child who chooses the wrong answer of C likely has a different misconception than the child who chooses the wrong answer of D. If you know why students are struggling, you can help them more effectively.
I reckon I have written over 10,000 multiple-choice diagnostic questions in the 10 years since I co-founded diagnosticquestions.com and Eedi. And to be honest, I need a break.

One of the golden rules for writing a good diagnostics question is you want each choice of the wrong answers to capture one and only one misconception so you can be confident in your diagnosis of where the student has gone wrong.

On a technical level, these AI chatbots are trained on large data sets comprised mainly of correct responses. Hence, the notion of thinking where students may go wrong and responding with an appropriate answer choice lies somewhat outside of their wheelhouse.

Most importantly, as we also saw last week, chatbots make mistakes, no matter how sure of themselves they initially sound. Unless you spot these mistakes and inform the chatbots, they will remain blissfully unaware.
